title: Pip’s Paint Playground
tagline: Mix a little paint. Discover a new color.
learningGoal: After watching a paint-mixing demonstration, choose yellow and blue as the two paints used to make the modeled green, even when their order or the painted object changes.
childTakeaway: These yellow and blue paints mix into green.
story: Pip wants green wings for a butterfly picture, but the art table has yellow and blue paint. The child helps Pip find, mix, and reuse the recipe.
introPip: Let’s paint a butterfly! I have yellow and blue paint. Help me find the yellow, then we’ll see what happens when we stir.
conceptImageAlt: Pip beside an outdoor art table with yellow and blue paint pots, a green mixing dish, a brush, and a butterfly painting with green wings.

ageSupport.entry: Read every color and choice aloud; show the full stirring demonstration after round 1. Permit replay anytime, adult co-exploration, and single taps rather than dragging.
ageSupport.stretch: Round 5 invites finding a missing ingredient. Keep it optional; do not add extra color recipes before demonstrating them.

misconception: Two colored areas being next to each other means they have already blended; the lesson makes stirring and a visible mixture explicit.

rounds.title: Find the first paint
rounds.sceneAlt: Two large paint pots: blue with a circle badge on the left and yellow with a triangle badge on the right. Pip waits above them.
rounds.success: That pot has yellow paint. Watch Pip stir a little yellow with a little blue. These paints make green!
hints: Listen as Pip names each pot: blue, then yellow.
Look at the yellow paint with the triangle badge.
This is the yellow pot. Now we can watch yellow and blue paint mix into green.
rounds.visualHint: Name and gently pulse each pot in turn. After selection, show separate yellow and blue paint dollops entering one dish, then a visible stirring sequence ending in green. The demonstration is required before round 2.
rounds.whyThisRound: Provides an easy color-identification entry and introduces the paint-mixing demonstration.

rounds.title: Predict the mix
rounds.prompt: Pip will stir yellow and blue paint. Which color do you think the mix will be?
rounds.sceneAlt: Yellow and blue paint pots above a covered mixing dish with a question mark. Below are yellow, green, and red sample choices. No output color is shown in the dish.
rounds.success: Yellow and blue made green in our paint dish. Let’s stir and check your prediction.
hints: We can replay Pip’s paint experiment.
Watch the yellow and blue dollops blend as Pip stirs.
The stirred paint is green. Choose the green sample with the leaf badge.
rounds.visualHint: Offer a replay of the actual yellow-and-blue stirring demonstration; uncover the output only after a prediction or requested hint.
rounds.whyThisRound: Asks for a prediction using the demonstrated recipe; it distinguishes the mixture from either original input.

rounds.title: Paint a butterfly
rounds.prompt: Pip wants green paint for this butterfly. Which two paints should Pip mix?
rounds.sceneAlt: A butterfly with green wings above two recipe cards: yellow plus yellow on the left, blue plus yellow on the right.
rounds.success: Blue and yellow make our green paint. Changing which pot comes first does not change this recipe.
hints: The butterfly needs the green paint we made.
Our green recipe uses two different paints.
Mix blue and yellow. They are the same two paints we used before, in the other order.
rounds.visualHint: Replay the two input dollops in swapped order; show them stir into the same modeled green.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfers the recipe to a new object and reversed input order; checks that two yellow portions are not treated as green.

rounds.title: Together or mixed?
rounds.prompt: Which dish shows the yellow and blue paints stirred together?
rounds.sceneAlt: Two dishes of paint. The left dish has one smooth green color. The right dish has separate yellow and blue halves touching at the center.

choices.label: Left dish: one green mixture
choices.spokenLabel: The left dish, with one green mixture

choices.label: Right dish: separate yellow and blue
choices.spokenLabel: The right dish, with separate yellow and blue

rounds.success: The green paint is mixed. In the other dish, yellow and blue are still separate. Pip needs to stir them.
hints: Look for one blended paint, instead of two separate patches.
Trace where yellow and blue still meet in the right dish. They have not blended yet.
The left dish is green all across. The right dish still has separate yellow and blue.
rounds.visualHint: Trace the unmixed boundary, then animate a spoon blending the right dish. Do not imply paint changes merely because two patches touch.
rounds.whyThisRound: Reveals the misconception that nearby colors automatically become a mixture.

rounds.title: Finish the green recipe
rounds.prompt: Pip already has blue paint. Which paint should Pip add to make our green?
rounds.sceneAlt: A blue paint pot beside an unknown ingredient and a green target sample. The three choices below are red, blue, and yellow paint pots.
rounds.success: Add yellow to the blue. Those two paints make our green again. Now Pip can finish the butterfly.
hints: One part of our green recipe is already here: blue.
Replay the recipe and watch which other pot joins blue.
Blue needs yellow for this recipe. Choose the yellow pot with the triangle badge.
rounds.visualHint: Replay the recipe and visually leave the yellow ingredient slot open; after a choice, fill the slot and stir.
rounds.whyThisRound: Optional backward reasoning: supplies the missing ingredient instead of choosing a complete recipe.

finale: Pip uses the mixed green paint to finish the butterfly wings. The child can replay the stir and choose another outline to paint with the same mixture.
offlineActivity: With a grown-up, use small amounts of washable yellow and blue paint on a reusable dish. Predict, stir, and describe the green you actually see. Try reversing the order. Use suitable art materials, keep paint out of mouths, and wash hands afterward.
reviewQuestions: Is yellow-and-blue-to-green enough for the first lesson, or do you want a separately demonstrated red-and-yellow-to-orange extension later?
Does the butterfly story make mixing feel purposeful, or would a vehicle-painting story fit Pip’s world better?
Should children who cannot reliably distinguish these colors get an adult-supported explore mode with spoken names and recipe badges, instead of scored color identification?
designNotes: Standalone adult review concept only. No game integration or child-testing evidence.
Generated illustration is introductory story art. Exact round SVGs define the learning questions.

The green is a simplified result for selected yellow and blue paints; actual pigments, proportions, and lighting affect shade and saturation. Test the chosen physical paints before filming or implementing the demonstration.
This teaches paint mixing. Do not reuse the recipe for colored light or blend screen RGB inputs as if that models pigments.
Prediction round 2 displays two inputs and an unknown output; the green option is a choice, not a revealed result.

Color names are read aloud. Persistent badges provide redundant identification: yellow triangle, blue circle, green leaf, red square. The badges are arbitrary identifiers, not a claim that real colors have shapes.

Labels and badges help follow a known recipe but cannot make color discrimination universally accessible. Offer an unscored narrated explore path or adult co-play; do not assess a child’s understanding solely by hue recognition.

Round 4 also offers spatial labels and a visible separate-color boundary. Its spoken description supports access but may reveal the answer; prioritize access over treating it as an independent assessment.

All answer cards have equal neutral borders. No correct-answer highlight in unassisted SVGs. Prompt playback, choice reading, and stirring are design intentions only; this review pack does not produce audio or run a child experience.

sources.title: Crayola: What are the primary colors?
sources.supports: Primary art-material maker’s conventional color-mixing relationship yellow + blue = green. Checked September 30, 2026. This supports the basic paint recipe, not identical results across every pigment or light mixing.
